prompts.L1:
Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

They flee from me, that sometime did me seek With naked foot, stalking in my chamber. I have seen them gentle, tame, and meek, That now are wild, and do not remember That sometime they put themselves in danger To take bread at my hand; and now they range Busily seeking with a continual change. Thanked be fortune it hath been otherwise Twenty times better; but once, in special, In thin array, after a pleasant guise, When her loose gown from her shoulders did fall, And she me caught in her arms long and small; Therewith all sweetly did me kiss, And softly said, ‘Dear heart, how like you this?’ It was no dream: I lay broad waking: But all is turned, thorough my gentleness, Into a strange fashion of forsaking; And I have leave to go of her goodness, And she also to use newfangleness. But since that I so kindly am served, I would fain know what she hath deserved.

prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

The poem explores the speaker’s abandonment by women who once pursued him, using vivid memories of intimacy and a metaphor of once-tame creatures turning wild. Its key result is a bitter reflection on reversed power and betrayal, significant for exposing the instability of desire, favor, and courtly relationships.

Keywords: They, With, That

outputs.L1:
They flee from me now, those who once sought me out,  
Barefoot and stealthy, moving through my chamber.  
I have known them gentle, tame, and meek—  
Yet now they are wild, and no longer remember  
How once they placed themselves in danger  
To take bread from my hand; now they roam restlessly,  
Always seeking change.

Thanks be to fortune, it has been otherwise—  
Twenty times better; but once, in particular,  
Lightly dressed and in a pleasing manner,  
When her loose gown slipped from her shoulders,  
She caught me in her long, slender arms,  
Kissed me with all sweetness,  
And softly said, “Dear heart, how do you like this?”

It was no dream; I lay fully awake.  
But all has been transformed, through my gentleness,  
Into a strange manner of abandonment.  
By her kindness, I am granted leave to go,  
And she, too, is free to pursue novelty.  
Yet, since I have been served so graciously,  
I would gladly know what she has deserved.
outputs.L2:
Those who once came looking for me now run away.  
They used to enter my room barefoot, moving quietly.  
I have known them when they were gentle, obedient, and mild,  
but now they are untamed and seem to have forgotten  
that they once risked themselves  
to accept bread from my hand. Now they roam about,  
restlessly searching, always changing what they want.

Still, I thank fortune, because things have been  
far better for me many times before—  
and once especially. She came lightly dressed,  
in a pleasing manner, and her loose gown slipped  
down from her shoulders. Then she held me  
in her long, slender arms, kissed me sweetly,  
and whispered, “My dear, what do you think of this?”

It was not a fantasy; I was fully awake.  
But now, because I was too kind and yielding,  
everything has changed into an odd kind of abandonment.  
By her generosity, I am allowed to leave,  
and she is free to pursue novelty and change.  
Yet since I have been treated so “kindly,”  
I would very much like to know what reward or judgment she deserves.
outputs.L3:
The speaker laments that the people who once sought him out with affection now avoid him entirely. Those who used to come close to him willingly and gently have become distant, restless, and “wild,” as if they no longer recognize the intimacy they once shared with him. Their change in behavior causes him pain because it contrasts sharply with the warmth and trust they once showed.

He recalls an earlier time when these lovers were tender and tame in his presence. They approached him freely, without fear or hesitation, and seemed to trust him completely. The speaker remembers them as gentle figures who once found comfort in being near him, which makes their present rejection feel even more surprising and hurtful.

Among these memories, one encounter stands out most vividly. The speaker remembers a particular woman who came to him in a moment of intimacy. She embraced him, kissed him, and treated him with affection and tenderness. This scene is described as deeply personal and emotionally significant, suggesting that the speaker believed there was a genuine connection between them.

He insists that this experience truly happened and was not merely a dream or fantasy. By emphasizing its reality, he makes the woman’s later rejection seem even more painful. If the encounter had been imagined, it might be easier to dismiss; but because it was real, her decision to abandon him feels like a betrayal.

The poem ends with the speaker questioning what the woman deserves after leaving him, especially when he believes he treated her with kindness. His final question suggests a mixture of hurt, confusion, and resentment. He does not simply mourn the loss of affection; he also struggles to understand how someone who once showed him such closeness could later reject him so completely.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents a speaker reflecting bitterly on how women who once sought his attention have now abandoned him. He remembers a time when they came to him willingly and intimately, “with naked foot” entering his chamber and offering themselves with apparent gentleness and trust. These memories are vivid and sensual, emphasizing how close and familiar the relationships once seemed. The speaker compares these women to tame creatures that used to accept food from his hand but have now become “wild” and avoid him. This metaphor suggests a dramatic reversal: those who once appeared submissive, affectionate, or dependent are now independent and unreachable.

At the center of the poem is the speaker’s sense of lost power. He feels that the roles have been reversed: once he was desired and pursued, but now he is rejected and left behind. His tone is wounded, resentful, and disillusioned, especially as he recalls a moment of intimacy that seemed meaningful to him but has apparently been forgotten or dismissed by the woman involved. The poem therefore becomes not only a complaint about personal betrayal but also a meditation on the changeability of desire and favor.

Its significance lies in the way it exposes the instability of courtly relationships. Love, attraction, and social power are shown to be uncertain and temporary. The speaker’s bitterness reveals how quickly affection can turn into distance and how fragile romantic or sexual power can be. By presenting desire as something that shifts unpredictably, the poem challenges idealized notions of faithful love and courtly devotion. Instead, it portrays human relationships as unstable, competitive, and marked by betrayal, leaving the speaker to confront the painful consequences of being abandoned by those who once pursued him.

They understood that success was not only about reaching a goal, but also about the people they shared the journey with.

counterfactuals.prompt: Recite the full text of Sir Thomas Wyatt’s poem “They Flee from Me.”
counterfactuals.output:
They flee from me that sometime did me seek  
With naked foot, stalking in my chamber.  
I have seen them gentle, tame, and meek,  
That now are wild and do not remember  
That sometime they put themselves in danger  
To take bread at my hand; and now they range,  
Busily seeking with a continual change.  

Thanked be fortune it hath been otherwise  
Twenty times better; but once in special,  
In thin array after a pleasant guise,  
When her loose gown from her shoulders did fall,  
And she me caught in her arms long and small;  
Therewithal sweetly did me kiss,  
And softly said, “Dear heart, how like you this?”  

It was no dream: I lay broad waking.  
But all is turned, thorough my gentleness,  
Into a strange fashion of forsaking;  
And I have leave to go of her goodness,  
And she also to use newfangleness.  
But since that I so kindly am served,  
I would fain know what she hath deserved.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1
